senses.subdomain: Low Status or Rank [including persons of low status]
senses.def: pertaining to being obscure or insignificant, with the possible implication of lacking in noble descent
pertaining to being impossible, presumably because of a lack of power to alter or control circumstances
senses.comment: In view of the double negation in Luke 1:37, it is often better to translate it as a positive statement, for example, ‘God can do anything.’

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: pertaining to an unlimited duration of time
senses.comment: The most frequent use of αἰώνιος in the NT is with ζωή 'life', for example, ἵνα πᾶς ὁ πιστεύων ἐν αὐτῷ ἔχω ζωὴν αἰώνιον ‘so that everyone who believes in him may have eternal life’ John 3:15. In combination with ζωή there is evidently not only a temporal element, but also a qualitative distinction. In such contexts, αἰώνιος evidently carries certain implications associated with αἰώνιος in relationship to divine and supernatural attributes. If one translates ‘eternal life’ as simply ‘never dying,’ there may be serious misunderstandings, since persons may assume that ‘never dying’ refers only to physical existence rather than to ‘spiritual death.’ Accordingly, some translators have rendered ‘eternal life’ as ‘unending real life,’ so as to introduce a qualitative distinction.

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
senses.def: an exceedingly long period of time from an assumed beginning up to the present
that which has been ritually defiled
to put on clothes, implying the clothing being completely around; see also 49.5
to put on clothing to adorn the outward form of something
a relation of proportion
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand ἀναλογία in Romans 12:6 as meaning ‘in agreement with,’ but this meaning likewise involves a degree of isomorphic relationship.

senses.def: pertaining to not being possible, in the sense of not being in accord with human experience
senses.comment: In view of the double negation in Luke 17:1, it may be better to translate ‘things that make people fall into sin are bound to happen.’ The derivative meaning of ἀνένδεκτος in the context of Luke 17:1 is thus a matter of inevitability as based upon human experience (see 71.38).

senses.def: a dispute involving opposite opinions
(derivative of ἀντιλέγω ‘to speak against,’ 33.455) a contradiction involving a contrary statement or evidence
rebellion against authority, with special focus upon verbal opposition

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to not being able to be tempted
senses.comment: There may be some difficulties involved in rendering the passive expression in James 1:13, but it is often possible to restructure this as an active expression with an indefinite person made the subject, for example, ‘no one can tempt God to do what is bad.’ It is also possible to shift the meaning slightly in terms of desire or will and thus say ‘God would never want to do what is evil.’

senses.def: to cause to roll away from a particular point
act of destroying or causing the destruction of persons, objects, or institutions
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is difficult to find a general term for ‘destruction.’ What has often happened is the extension of meaning from a more specific type of reference, for example, ‘to smash,’ to a more generic meaning of ‘to destroy,’ and whether one understands the specific or more generic meaning depends largely upon the context. Accordingly, in Acts 8:3 one may find a figurative usage of a term meaning ‘to smash’ (though understood in a more generic sense), for example, ‘Saul then worked in order to smash the church.’

senses.def: an action demonstrating complete disregard for the value of something
senses.comment: In the context of Mark 14:4 the understanding of ἀπώλεια in the literal sense of ‘destruction’ (see 20.31) does not seem to be adequate. The following verse concerning the three hundred denarii would seem to indicate that it was disregard for the value of something rather than destroying the perfume. In fact, the use of the perfume would not have been a matter of destroying. Accordingly, an equivalent of ‘waste’ seems to be far more satisfactory. In some languages the equivalent of this question in Mark 14:4 is ‘why did she not think about the value of the perfume?’

senses.def: the son of Herod I

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to act in defiance of social and moral standards, with resulting disgrace, embarrassment, and shame
senses.comment: Behavior involving disgrace, embarrassment, and shame is often expressed in an idiomatic manner, for example, ‘to bury one’s face,’ ‘to hide one’s eyes,’ or ‘to feel stabbed by people’s eyes.’ Since shame is seemingly a universal type of feeling, there is usually no difficulty involved in obtaining a satisfactory equivalent.

senses.def: a state which is or should be regarded as causing shame
to be like or similar to something else
to rule as a king, with the implication of complete authority and the possibility of being able to pass on the right to rule to one’s son or near kin
senses.comment: It is generally a serious mistake to translate the phrase ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ ‘the kingdom of God’ as referring to a particular area in which God rules. The meaning of this phrase in the NT involves not a particular place or special period of time but the fact of ruling. An expression such as ‘to enter the kingdom of God’ thus does not refer to ‘going to heaven’ but should be understood as ‘accepting God’s rule’ or ‘welcoming God to rule over.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of βασιλεύω[a] ‘to rule, to reign as a king,’ 37.64) to be in control in an absolute manner
senses.comment: In a number of languages, however, it may be impossible to personify death as being capable of ‘reigning’ or ‘ruling.’ Sometimes the equivalent meaning may be expressed as ‘from the time of Adam to that of Moses there was no way for people to escape death’ or ‘… to die was certain’ (Romans 5:14).

senses.def: (derivative of βλασφημέω ‘to blaspheme,’ 33.400) pertaining to being insulting and slanderous
(derivative of Γαλατία ‘Galatia,’ 93.442) a person who is a native of Galatia
to express one’s discontent
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be necessary to restructure ‘complaint’ as a verb rather than as a noun, and therefore this expression in Acts 6:1 may be rendered as ‘Greek-speaking Jews complained against what the local Jews were doing.’

senses.def: a meal whether simple or elaborate (this generic meaning of δεῖπνον is in contrast with the more specific meaning of δεῖπνον[b], 23.25)
senses.comment: Though ἄριστον[a], δεῖπνον[a], and βρῶσις[b] are highly generic in this usage, it is not necessary to translate these terms by a corresponding generic term in another language, since a more specific term may fit the context more satisfactorily. In fact, a generic term might be quite inappropriate in that it would suggest in the case of Mark 6:21 that Herod was quite stingy in simply providing an ordinary meal for his officials.

senses.def: the principal meal of the day, usually in the evening
senses.comment: Though in the so-called Western world there is a tendency to have three meals each day, breakfast, lunch, and dinner (or supper), in many parts of the world there are only two principal meals: one eaten around nine or ten o’clock in the morning, and another at four or five o’clock in the afternoon.|In some languages there is a very important distinction made between a more or less formal meal and the relatively informal times of eating which might be called ‘snacks.’ These would be occasions on which one would eat only one kind of food and possibly in relatively small quantities.

senses.def: an elaborate meal
to give something to a series of persons
to dispose of one’s property by means of a will
senses.comment: ‘To make a will’ may be rendered as ‘to write out a will’ or ‘to say who is to receive one’s property after one dies.’

senses.def: to make a solemn agreement involving reciprocal benefits and responsibilities

senses.subdomain: Assign to a Role or Function
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to designate ruling) to designate someone in a somewhat formal or official way for the role of ruling
glosses: to give the right to rule
to provide with the authority to rule
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be difficult to translate literally ‘to give the right to rule.’ Often this is expressed by direct discourse, for example, ‘to say, You now have the authority to rule’ or ‘to say, You are now able to command.’

senses.subdomain: Once, Twice, Three Times, Etc. [Cardinals of Time]
senses.def: two occurrences

senses.subdomain: Once, Twice, Three Times, Etc. [Cardinals of Time]
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: once and twice) an indefinite low number, but more than once
(an idiom, literally: dying twice) the state of being completely dead
senses.comment: The phrase δὶς ἀποθανόντα in Jude 1:12 refers specifically to trees, but figuratively to persons. It is possible that δὶς ἀποθανόντα is applicable to trees (1) on the basis that they die while still standing and (2) that death is fully confirmed by their being rooted up, but in view of the figurative context, it is better to translate δὶς ἀποθανόντα as simply ‘completely dead.’

senses.def: pertaining to being understandable, but only with great effort

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: the largest unit into which the people of the world are divided on the basis of their constituting a socio-political community
senses.comment: In a number of languages a term meaning basically ‘tribe’ has been extended in meaning to identify ‘nations.’ In other instances different nations are spoken of simply as ‘different peoples.’ In certain cases distinct nations are classified primarily in terms of their diverse languages, for example, ‘those people who speak different languages.’ Such an expression should not, however, be used if it only refers to multilingual persons.

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: (an extended meaning of ἔθνος ‘nation,’ 11.55) those who do not belong to the Jewish or Christian faith
senses.comment: Though in a number of instances τὰ ἔθνη may be rendered as ‘those who do not believe in God,’ it is often more appropriate to render τὰ ἔθνη in terms of belief in other gods or in false gods. For example, Ephesians 4:17 may be rendered as ‘do not any longer live like those who believe in idols’ or ‘… in gods who are not really God.’

senses.def: to remove clothing from the body (as a reverse process of ἐνδύω ‘to put on,’ 49.1)
to wrench or sprain the ligaments of a joint, especially in the legs and feet
senses.comment: It is often possible to speak of ‘being wrenched’ as ‘being twisted.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ἐκτρέπομαι ‘to turn from,’ not occurring in the NT) to turn away from the truth and to believe something which is different
glosses: to turn from and to follow

senses.def: to avoid becoming involved in some type of activity
to dip an object in a liquid
to be inside an area or object
glosses: to be inside (in the participial forms: what is inside, contents)

senses.def: to leap up to a standing position
senses.comment: It is possible that in Acts 3:8 the paralyzed man actually jumped up from the ground, but it is more likely that the reference is to the rapidity with which he got onto his feet.

senses.def: to go back toward or to some point or area (perhaps somewhat more emphatic than the series in 15.89 in view of the prepositional prefix ἐπ)
to leave the shore for a point out in the water or in the direction of open water
glosses: to put out to open water
to go away from the shore

senses.def: to use an attribution in speaking of a person
senses.comment: It is not always possible to determine from the context whether the act involved is an initial naming of a person or simply calling a person by a particular name. Likewise in the case of attributions or titles, it is not always possible to determine whether it is a matter of giving an attribution or title to a person or simply a matter of speaking of or to a person by means of such an attribution or title. In some instances the giving of a title may be made indirect. For example, in Matthew 1:23 the statement ‘and they will call his name Emmanuel’ suggests the giving of a title, but the process is stated in terms of how people will speak of this person.

senses.def: to call upon someone to do something, normally implying an appeal for aid
senses.comment: ἐπικαλέομαι[a] also occurs in such expressions as ὅς ἂν ἐπικαλέσηται τὸ ὄνομα κυρίου (Acts 2:21) ‘whoever calls upon the name of the Lord,’ but the meaning is essentially the same as ‘to call upon the Lord,’ since τὸ ὄνομα ‘the name’ may simply be a metonym for ‘the Lord.’

senses.def: to claim one’s legal right to have a case reviewed by a higher tribunal
glosses: to appeal to a higher court
senses.comment: The second clause in Acts 26:32 may also be rendered in a number of languages as ‘if he had not asked for the Emperor to listen to his case’ or ‘… to judge the accusations against him.’

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to have someone’s name called upon someone) to be acknowledged as belonging to the one whose name is called upon such an individual
senses.comment: This interpretation of the expression ἐπικαλέομαι τὸ ὄνομά τινος ἐπί τινα is based upon well attested OT usage, and though it is quite different from traditional interpretations of Acts 9:14 and Acts 15:17, it should be followed as reflecting a more satisfactory and accurate interpretation of the passive form of ἐπικαλέω.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ἐπισωρεύω ‘to heap up,’ not occurring in the NT) to significantly increase the number of something
a flat piece of highly polished metal used to reflect an image
to experience and enjoy favorable circumstances
senses.comment: In a number of languages εὐοδόομαι in 3 John 1:2 is expressed idiomatically, for example, ‘to always eat well’ or ‘to live under the shade’ or ‘to live always with laughter and song.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of εὐοδόομαι ‘to travel along a good road,’ not occurring in the NT) to be successful in acquiring profit or gain
to be successful in accomplishing some activity or event
pertaining to being hot, often associated with boiling
senses.comment: In Revelation 3:15 the usage is figurative; ζεστός in the sense of a favorable attitude towards something seems not to have been a conventionalized meaning.|In a number of languages the contrast between ‘hot’ and ‘cold’ may refer primarily to sex or anger, in which case the contrast is certainly not appropriate for Revelation 3:15. It may therefore be necessary in many instances to use an equivalent such as ‘for or against’ or ‘friendly to or hostile toward.’

senses.def: to be at rest, that is, not to be engaged in some activity

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to live in a quiet, peaceful, mild manner
to maintain a state of silence, with a possible focus upon the attitude involved

a case or bag about the size and shape of a sword, used to cover and to carry the sword; made of leather, cloth, metal, or even wood; attached to a strap or belt that could be hung over the shoulder or tied around the waist
senses.comment: In this one occurrence of θήκη in the NT, the reference is to a ‘sheath’ for a sword, which may be rendered in some languages as ‘a leather bag for a sword’ or ‘a covering for a sword’ or ‘something in which a sword is carried.’

senses.def: a mountainous region south of Judea (Edom of the OT)

senses.subdomain: Same or Equivalent Kind or Class
senses.def: pertaining to that which is equal, either in number, size, quality, or characteristics
a degree of totality or completeness
(derivative of καρποφορέω[a] ‘to produce seed,’ 23.199) pertaining to producing seed or harvest
senses.comment: In some instances it may be useful to translate ‘fruitful seasons’ as ‘seasons when crops become ripe’ or even ‘the time of the year when there is always plenty to eat.’

senses.def: to remain in the same place over a period of time
to move down, irrespective of the gradient
senses.comment: In a number of languages there is a series of terms for going down or descending, depending upon the gradient and the rapidity with which someone or something descends. There may also be distinct terms depending upon the extent of the descent. Rain coming down would be regarded as an extensive descent, while getting out of a boat to walk on the water would be a very limited descent.|Movement downward may, of course, involve more than physical objects, for example, οὐκ ἔστιν αὕτη ἡ σοφία ἄνωθεν κατερχομένη ‘this is not the wisdom that comes down from above’ James 3:15. Since in James 3:15 ἄνωθεν is a substitute for God, it may be necessary to restructure this statement as ‘this wisdom does not come from God’ or ‘God is not the source of this wisdom.’

senses.def: (technical, nautical term) to go by ship toward the shore

senses.subdomain: Instruments Used in Marking and Writing
senses.def: section of a scroll or of a long composition
senses.comment: Long compositions often involved several scrolls, and a κεφαλίς would form one section or scroll of such a composition.|In the case of practically all terms for documents (for example, ‘letter,’ ‘book,’ ‘scroll’) the meaning involves not only the object on which the writing was done, but also the contents of the writing. In some languages a distinction must be made between these two aspects of such objects, and one must make certain that the particular expression used in a receptor language will at least include the contents and not refer merely to the materials on which the words may have been written.

senses.def: the state of being asleep
senses.comment: In some languages sleep is expressed by an idiom, for example, ‘his soul had wandered away’ or ‘his eyes had disappeared.’ Though an expression such as ‘his soul had wandered away’ might appear in some languages to have misleading theological implications, it really means only ‘to sleep.’|In John 11:13 κοίμησις is combined with ὕπνος apparently to stress the fact that the sleep was an ordinary or natural sleep.

senses.def: to become strong and healthy, with the implication of physical vigor
senses.comment: In employing an expression to translate ‘to become strong,’ it is important to avoid the impression of ‘to become muscular.’ The emphasis is upon total physical vigor, not mere muscular strength.

senses.def: (derivative of κραταιός ‘powerful,’ 76.9) to become strong psychologically
senses.comment: In 1 Corinthians 16:13 κραταιόομαι must be understood in a non-physical sense. The implication is that the believer is to be sufficiently strong as to be able to dominate any evil influence.

senses.def: to invest something with power or force
senses.comment: In order to express the meaning of this phrase in Galatians 3:15, it may be necessary in some languages to make more specific the arrangements involved, for example, ‘if people have signed an agreement, no one can disregard it’ or ‘if an agreement has been confirmed, no one can say it does not exist’ or, as in some languages, ‘if an agreement has been tied, no one can untie it.’

senses.def: to cause someone to recognize the reality of something
glosses: to show something to be real

senses.def: to receive or accept an object or benefit for which the initiative rests with the giver, but the focus of attention in the transfer is upon the receiver
the nephew of Abraham
to beat severely with a whip
a state of disease, often implying divine punishment
a point or region of the sky directly above the earth

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: a state of being tainted or stained by evil
(derivative of μύρον ‘perfume,’ 6.205) to anoint with perfumed oil or ointment, often in connection with burial

(a figurative extension of meaning of νήφω ‘to be sober, to not be drunk,’ probably not occurring in the NT; see 88.86) to be in control of one’s thought processes and thus not be in danger of irrational thinking
glosses: to be well composed in mind
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand νήφω in 1 Thessalonians 5:6 as meaning ‘self-control,’ as a characteristic of moral behavior (see 88.86).

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of νήφω ‘to be sober,’ in the sense of ‘not being drunk,’ probably not occurring in the NT) to behave with restraint and moderation, thus not permitting excess
glosses: to be moderate in one’s behavior
senses.comment: It is possible that in 1 Thessalonians 5:8 νήφω means lack of drunkenness, but most scholars interpret the use of νήφω in the NT as applying to a broader range of soberness or sobriety, namely, restraint and moderation which avoids excess in passion, rashness, or confusion. For another interpretation of νήφω in 1 Thessalonians 5:8, as well as in 1 Thessalonians 5:6, see 30.25.

senses.def: eighth in a series involving either time, space, or set
senses.comment: In a number of languages one does not speak of ‘the eighth’ as being the eighth item in a set. Often it is far more usual to say ‘one together with seven others.’ This same system may apply to all ordinals in a language.

senses.def: a degree of completeness, with the possible implication of purpose or result
pertaining to an area characterized by mountains or hills
a marker of a somewhat more emphatically negativized proposition

senses.subdomain: Markers for an Affirmative Response to Questions
senses.def: a marker of a somewhat more emphatic affirmative response
to act contrary to established custom or law, with the implication of intent
senses.comment: Languages differ appreciably in the way in which they speak of disobeying or transgressing a law. It is rarely possible to speak of ‘breaking a law,’ since nothing is actually done to the law in the process of transgression, but languages do employ such expressions as ‘to tramp on a law,’ ‘to ridicule a law,’ and ‘to laugh at a law.’ See also discussion at 36.29.

senses.def: to think or reason in a completely irrational manner
glosses: to not be in one’s right mind
to be out of one’s mind
senses.comment: It may be necessary in some languages to restructure the expression ‘stopped the prophet’s insane action.’ This can often be done by saying ‘prevented the prophet from acting like a crazy person.’ In other languages παραφρονία is best rendered by an idiomatic expression such as ‘wandering thoughts’ or ‘twisted thoughts.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of παχύνομαι ‘to become thick,’ not occurring in the NT) to become unable to understand or comprehend as the result of being mentally dull or spiritually insensitive
to remain in a place and/or state, with expectancy concerning a future event
a region in central Asia Minor
(derivative of ποιμαίνω[a] ‘to take care of sheep or goats,’ 44.3) one who takes care of sheep or goats
(a figurative extension of meaning of ποιμήν[a] ‘shepherd,’ 44.4) one who is responsible for the care and guidance of a Christian congregation
senses.comment: Note that in Ephesians 4:11 there are four classes of persons, not five, for the last class involves two complementary roles, that of pastor and teacher, in other words, to guide and help a congregation as well as to teach.

senses.def: to be engaged in some kind of business, generally buying and selling
to change one’s state for the better by advancing and making progress
to progress or advance in some activity
to cause a significant increase in some quantity
senses.comment: This expression in 2 Timothy 2:16 may be rendered in some languages as ‘they cause people to be more and more godless’ or ‘… to do what God does not want them to do.’

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
senses.def: to extend in time, with focus upon the end point

senses.subdomain: Belong To, Be Included in the Membership of, Be Excluded From
senses.def: the acceptance of someone into an association
senses.comment: In rendering this expression in Romans 11:15 it may be necessary to indicate clearly the participants involved. For example, one may translate ‘what will happen when God accepts them? It will be the same as having risen from the dead’ or ‘… will be the resurrection of the dead.’

senses.def: (derivative of πτοέομαι ‘to be terrified,’ 25.264) an object, event, or condition that causes terror or alarm
glosses: something that causes one to be afraid

senses.def: to tear, rip, or burst, either from internal or external forces, with the implication of sudden and forceful action
to suddenly break out into shouting
senses.comment: In Galatians 4:27 the combination ῥῆξον καὶ βόησον may be analyzed either as two expressions for shouting, for example, ‘break into shouting and shout,’ or ῥῆξον may function primarily as an aspectual qualifier of βόησον, so that the meaning of the expression ῥῆξον καὶ βόησον may be ‘break into shouting’ or ‘begin to shout,’ but the beginning of shouting would imply considerable energy, spontaneity, and suddenness. For this interpretation of ῥήγνυμι in Galatians 4:27, see 68.81.

senses.def: to do something rapidly and with considerable energy or effort
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ῥήγνυμι in Galatians 4:27, see 33.85.

senses.def: to cause to fall to the ground in convulsions

pertaining to being of poor or bad quality and hence of little or no value (particularly in reference to plants, either in the sense of seriously diseased or of seedling stock, that is, not budded or grafted)
senses.comment: Some scholars have suggested that σαπρός in Matthew 7:18 really refers to a seedling, that is to say, a tree which has grown up completely from seed rather than being budded or grafted. Seedling trees often produce tasteless or even bitter fruit. By its very nature, such a tree cannot produce good fruit and is, therefore, considered to be of no value.

senses.def: pertaining to that which is harmful in view of its being unwholesome and corrupting
senses.comment: In Ephesians 4:29 σαπρός is in contrast with that which is ἀγαθός ‘good’ for building up what is necessary. In such a context ἀγαθός may be interpreted as that which is helpful, and by contrast σαπρός may be understood to mean ‘harmful.’

senses.def: to sift by shaking in a sieve
senses.comment: The expression ὑμᾶς τοῦ σινιάσαι ὡς τὸν σῖτον in Luke 22:31 is clearly a type of figurative usage and in many languages must be translated as ‘to test you’ or ‘to test you so as to separate the good from the bad.’ In some languages, however, it may be more satisfactory to shift the figure from sifting to winnowing and hence translate ‘to winnow you like a farmer who separates the wheat from the chaff.’

senses.def: to cause a person to have wisdom and understanding
(derivative of σοφία[c] ‘specialized knowledge, skill,’ 28.8) to have specialized knowledge involving the capacity to produce what is cleverly or skillfully made
glosses: to know how to create skillfully
to know how to contrive cleverly

senses.subdomain: Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period
senses.def: an extremely short unit of time
one who is closely linked with another in some activity
senses.comment: Some scholars, however, interpret σύζυγος in Philippians 4:3 as being a proper name.

senses.def: to settle or check on accounts with someone

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Duration of Time: Beginning, End
senses.def: to cause a duration to come to an abrupt end, with the implication of sooner than expected
senses.comment: There are a number of different opinions with regard to the meaning of συντέμνω in Romans 9:28. Translators are accordingly encouraged to consult commentaries and to provide for significantly different interpretations in translations.

senses.def: to have understanding about practical matters and thus be able to act sensibly

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to behave in a sensible manner, with the implication of thoughtful awareness of what is best

senses.subdomain: Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
senses.def: pertaining to the fourth in a series of days
to shake or tremble, often with the implication of fear and/or consternation
senses.comment: In a number of languages there are two distinct terms for trembling, one relating to illness (as in the case of epileptic seizures or the chills and fever associated with malaria) and the other associated with fear.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of τρέμω[a] ‘to tremble,’ 16.6) to be so afraid as to tremble, often with the implication of awe
senses.comment: For another interpretation of τρέμω in 2 Peter 2:10, see 87.14.

senses.subdomain: Honor or Respect in Relation to Status
senses.def: to have such awe or respect for a person as to involve a measure of fear
senses.comment: In a number of languages there are serious problems involved in speaking of ‘fearing God,’ for this might imply merely ‘to be scared of God’ as though God were some kind of bogeyman. If there is a term with the meaning of ‘awe’ (perhaps in a phrase such as ‘to stand in awe of’), this may be an adequate equivalent. In some instances awe is expressed idiomatically as ‘to stand with one’s heart in one’s throat’ or ‘to be in someone’s presence with one’s heart beating fast.’|For another interpretation of τρέμω in 2 Peter 2:10, see 25.259.

In a number of languages ‘to drink water’ is expressed by a single term which combines the components of drinking and of water. In other instances a verb meaning simply ‘to drink’ normally means to drink water unless otherwise specified. In Greek almost the opposite situation exists. For example, Matthew 11:18 (ἦλθεν γὰρ Ἰωάννης μήτε ἐσθίων μήτε πίνων ‘for John came neither eating nor drinking’) implies a reference to drinking alcoholic beverages.

senses.def: an animal which can be used to carry a burden or can be ridden
senses.comment: In Matthew 21:5 it may not actually be necessary to translate ‘the offspring of a beast of burden’ (υἱὸν ὑποζυγίου), since this may be regarded as being completely redundant after speaking of a donkey and her colt. In some languages it may be necessary in certain contexts to indicate the sex of a donkey. In 2 Peter 2:16 the reference of ὑποζύγιον is a female donkey, as indicated in the Hebrew text of.

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a member of an important religious and political Jewish party at the time of Jesus and the apostles. The Pharisees constituted a significantly larger group than the Sadducees (see 11.48) and differed with them on certain doctrines and patterns of behavior. The Pharisees were strict and jealous adherents to the laws of the OT and to numerous additional traditions
senses.comment: Translators have generally found it both wise and necessary to simply transliterate in one form or another Σαδδουκαῖος (11.48) and Φαρισαῖος, but some background information concerning these two parties is particularly important in a glossary; otherwise, certain passages of Scripture become extremely difficult to understand satisfactorily.

senses.def: to speak in such a way as to make no sense, presumably because of ignorance of what is involved
senses.comment: In some languages ‘to talk nonsense’ is ‘to talk without understanding what one is saying,’ but in other instances an equivalent may be ‘to talk without anybody being able to understand what one is saying.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of φωτισμός ‘light,’ not occurring in the NT) that which has been revealed as true
to cause something to be fully known by revealing clearly and in some detail
the husband of Joanna, a follower of Jesus
pertaining to being cold, as of weather conditions
